slides: Begin by placing the chapter inside the transition from projective conics to Euclidean metric geometry. The source span is PDF pages 227 through 263, while the notebook turns the chapter into inspectable focal and tangent experiments. The lecture question is not merely what conics are, but what new structure appears once distance, angle, and the cyclic points are available.

Emphasize that a projective conic does not already know its foci. The metric enters through an affine chart, the line at infinity, and the cyclic points that encode perpendicularity and angle. This is the main misconception to disarm before computations: focal formulas are not decorations on the equation, they are consequences of choosing Euclidean structure.

Use the ellipse slide to model the notebook rule of thumb: draw the locus, name the invariant, and then assert the quantity that should not change. The audience should inspect the two colored segments from a moving point to the foci. Their individual lengths vary, but their sum remains two a, which the notebook checks numerically.

The directrix definition gives a single metric sentence that separates ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas by eccentricity. Stress that the ratio uses Euclidean distance twice: from the point to the focus and from the point to the line. That makes it excellent for computation, but also reminds us that changing the metric changes the reading of the same algebraic curve.

Compare this slide directly with the ellipse slide. The construction uses the same code pattern and the same kind of colored distance segments, but the invariant has changed from a sum to an absolute difference. That small algebraic change is visible as two branches and asymptotic directions, giving students a concrete way to connect formula, topology, and drawing.

Here the invariant becomes a tangent statement. If the focal sum is constant, then any tiny motion along the ellipse has zero first-order change in that sum. The normal therefore points in the combined direction of the two unit focal vectors. That is the analytic reason the familiar optical reflection law belongs in a Euclidean conics chapter.

This is the bridge back to the previous projective conics chapter. The cyclic points are complex points on the line at infinity, so students should not look for them as real dots in the drawing. Their role is structural: they let Euclidean angle and circularity be described inside projective language, which explains why focal facts have projective shadows.

Move from points on the conic to lines touching the conic. This dual view is useful because several Euclidean constructions are easier to describe through tangent contact than through sampled points. The formula X transpose C Y equals zero is compact, but the diagram makes the meaning clear: the curve is the envelope organized by its tangent lines.

Confocal families are a good antidote to static definitions. When a parameter moves, students can see which features remain fixed and which ones respond. The foci and axes stay organized, while the visible curves change shape. This prepares the class for normal and tangent behavior, because the family acts like a coordinate web rather than isolated examples.

This table is meant as a measurement interface. Each normal form tells students what invariant to test and what visual feature should accompany it. The degenerate row is important because the chapter treats boundary cases as explanatory, not as errors. A dropped rank, tangent contact, or ideal direction often reveals why a theorem needs its hypotheses.

The lab slide explains how the notebook turns the chapter into a reproducible experiment. The code does not prove the focal theorems, but it makes the claims inspectable and falsifiable at the scale of the drawing. Ask students to predict what changes when parameters move, then use the residuals to decide whether their prediction respected the hypotheses.

Close by returning to the chapter question. Euclidean conics are not a separate species from projective conics; they are projective conics with metric information activated. The three durable ideas are metric enrichment, focal contracts, and tangent behavior. The suggested next inspection ties the point model and tangent model together in one computation.
